title: FOMC Minutes — June 16–17, 2026
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2026-06-17 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

Kevin Warsh chaired as Chairman (Jerome Powell had chaired in April). John Williams was Vice Chair, and Jerome Powell now voted as a Board member. The Committee held the federal funds range at 3.50–3.75%, and the vote was a unanimous 12–0. IORB stayed at 3.65% and the primary credit rate at 3.75%. The statement now says the Committee "will deliver price stability" and describes inflation as "elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal." The Committee agreed to drop the language signaling an easing bias, and a majority favored a shorter statement. This was an SEP meeting, with projections released after the meeting.

Economic outlook

Staff cut their GDP forecast slightly but still saw growth near potential this year and a bit above it over the next two years. Unemployment was expected to stay near its longer-run level and then dip slightly below it in 2028. Staff saw growth and employment risks tilted to the downside.

Inflation

Inflation got clearly worse. Headline PCE was 3.8% in April and core was 3.3%. Staff estimated May at 4.1% headline and 3.4% core. Drivers included tariff pass-through, Middle East energy costs and demand related to AI. Participants said price pressures had become more broad-based, and several noted that services inflation excluding housing had barely declined. Most warned that growth above potential could make inflation more persistent. Staff raised their inflation path and now saw about 2% only in 2028. Longer-term expectations stayed anchored near 2%.

Labor market

Unemployment was 4.3% in May and little changed over the past year. Payroll gains strengthened this year and were roughly in line with labor force growth. Some participants described a low-dynamism market with a lower job-finding rate. Others said earlier fears of deterioration had eased.

Financial markets & balance sheet

The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 20bp since April and about 50bp since the Middle East conflict began. The S&P 500 gained nearly 6% over the intermeeting period, led by technology. Private credit showed strain: inflows to business development companies slowed and redemption requests rose. Credit stayed tight for small businesses and lower-credit-score households. Reserve management purchases and reinvestment policy were unchanged. In mid-May, repo rates fell to 15bp below IORB, and modest reverse repo take-up confirmed the rate floor was working.

Risks participants flagged

  • Inflation persistence. Both staff and participants saw inflation risks skewed to the upside.
  • Commodity supply disruptions lasting longer than expected
  • AI-driven demand keeping prices for tech products and electricity elevated
  • Geopolitical uncertainty leading firms to cut hiring

What it signaled about next moves

All participants backed holding, but a few favored a hike already, though they did not press for one. Several said policy was not restrictive. Views on the year-end rate split: many saw it within or slightly below the current range, while many others saw it above. Almost all agreed that persistent inflation would likely call for some firming. The Chairman outlined five independent task forces to review how monetary policy is conducted.

Read-through for SPY

  • Dropping the easing bias under a new Chair formally ended the "cuts are coming" story. From here, the debate was hold versus hike.
  • Stocks still rallied nearly 6%, led by tech, even as 10-year yields rose. AI-driven earnings were outrunning higher rates for now.
  • Headline PCE above 4% and a Fed split on hikes raised the risk of a sharper repricing if inflation did not cool.
